svg.title: Cells
svg.desc: ANIMAL CELLS: Eukaryotic: DNA is enclosed in a nucleus. Nucleus → genetic material; controls activities through genes. Cytoplasm → many enzyme-controlled reactions. Membrane → controls entry and exit. Mitochondria → aerobic respiration transfers energy. Ribosomes → protein synthesis. PLANT CELLS: Also have a membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, mitochondria and ribosomes. Cellulose wall → strength and support. Algal cells also have cellulose walls. Permanent vacuole → cell sap; water helps keep the cell firm. Chloroplasts → photosynthesis; chlorophyll absorbs light. Chloroplasts occur in photosynthetic cells; root hair cells normally lack them. BACTERIAL CELLS: Prokaryotic and much smaller than plant or animal cells. No nucleus: one main DNA loop lies in the cytoplasm. Some have plasmids: small DNA rings carrying extra genes. Have a membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and a wall; the wall is not cellulose. No mitochondria or chloroplasts. SPERM CELLS: Tail → swimming towards the egg. Many mitochondria → respiration supplies energy for movement. Acrosome enzymes → help penetrate the egg's outer layers. Link each structure to its effect and the cell's job. NERVE & MUSCLE CELLS: Nerve cell: a long fibre carries electrical impulses over long distances. Branched ends connect with other cells. Muscle cell: contractile proteins allow shortening. Many mitochondria provide energy for contraction. ROOT HAIR CELLS: Long extension → large surface area for absorption. Water enters by osmosis. Mineral ions enter by active transport when their concentration is lower in the soil. Mitochondria supply energy from respiration for active transport. Underground → normally no chloroplasts. XYLEM & PHLOEM: Xylem: dead, hollow cells join into tubes → carry water and mineral ions. Lignin strengthens walls → support and resistance to collapse. Phloem: sieve tubes move dissolved sugars. Companion cells supply energy for loading sugars. Use feature → effect → function, including for unfamiliar cells. DIFFERENTIATION: A cell develops specialised structures to carry out a particular function. Most animal cells differentiate early in development. Many plant cells can differentiate throughout life. In mature animals, cell division mainly repairs and replaces cells. Remember: differentiation is the process; a specialised cell is the result.
